people/isaac-watts/summary: English Independent minister often called the father of English hymnody. His Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707) and The Psalms of David Imitated in the Language of the New Testament (1719) broke with the tradition of singing only metrical psalms, setting Christian experience to verse ("When I survey the wondrous cross").
people/john-williamson-nevin/summary: With Philip Schaff the leader of the "Mercersburg theology", which recovered catechesis, liturgy and a high view of the Lord’s Supper (The Mystical Presence, 1846). His The Anxious Bench (1843) criticised Finney-style revival techniques as manipulative and foreign to Reformed churchly piety.
people/john-williamson-nevin/keyIdeas/1: Mystical union and the real spiritual presence
people/marcel-lefebvre/roles/1: founder of the Society of St Pius X
people/marcel-lefebvre/summary: French missionary archbishop who opposed Vatican II’s teaching on religious liberty and ecumenism and the Mass of Paul VI. He founded the Society of St Pius X (1970) at Écône, Switzerland; his consecration of four bishops without papal mandate (1988) brought excommunication, which Benedict XVI lifted for the surviving bishops in 2009.
people/marcel-lefebvre/keyIdeas/0: Defence of the traditional Latin Mass
people/marcel-lefebvre/keyIdeas/1: Critique of religious liberty and ecumenism
people/benedict-xvi/roles/1: prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith
people/benedict-xvi/summary: German theologian, Vatican II peritus and later doctrinal prefect under John Paul II, elected pope in 2005. In The Spirit of the Liturgy (2000) and the motu proprio Summorum Pontificum (2007) he argued for a "hermeneutic of continuity" and freed the 1962 Missal as an "extraordinary form". He resigned in 2013.
people/benedict-xvi/keyIdeas/1: Two forms of the one Roman Rite
people/antony-the-great/summary: Egyptian Christian who withdrew to the desert c. 270-285 and became the archetypal hermit and 'father of monks'; Athanasius' Life of Antony spread his fame and the monastic ideal across the Christian world.
people/juan-diego/summary: Indigenous (Nahua) convert to whom, according to tradition first published in 1648-49, the Virgin of Guadalupe appeared at Tepeyac in 1531. His historicity is debated by historians; he was canonised by John Paul II in 2002.
people/jean-cavalier/summary: Huguenot baker's apprentice who became a leading commander of the Camisard revolt in the Cévennes (1702-04), in a movement inspired by ecstatic prophets; after negotiating with Marshal Villars he went into exile and ended his life as a British officer and lieutenant-governor of Jersey.
people/jean-cavalier/keyIdeas/0: Armed resistance to persecution of Huguenots
people/jean-cavalier/keyIdeas/1: Prophetic inspiration in the Camisard war
people/barton-w-stone/summary: Presbyterian minister who hosted the Cane Ridge camp meeting (1801), then left the Presbyterian synod and led the 'Christian' movement that merged in 1832 with Alexander Campbell's Disciples to form the Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement.
people/barton-w-stone/keyIdeas/0: Christian unity on the Bible alone
people/barton-w-stone/keyIdeas/2: Rejection of creeds as tests of fellowship
people/seraphim-of-sarov/summary: Russian monk and hermit of the Sarov monastery, famed as a spiritual elder, healer and teacher of the 'acquisition of the Holy Spirit'; canonised in 1903. Born in Kursk; his birth year is given as 1754 or 1759.
people/seraphim-of-sarov/keyIdeas/0: Acquisition of the Holy Spirit as the aim of Christian life
people/bernadette-soubirous/summary: Miller's daughter from Lourdes who reported eighteen apparitions of the Virgin Mary in 1858; she later became a Sister of Charity at Nevers and was canonised in 1933.
people/agnes-ozman/summary: Student at Charles Parham's Bethel Bible School in Topeka who, on 1 January 1901, became the first in Parham's circle to speak in tongues, an event central to the formulation of the Pentecostal 'initial evidence' doctrine.
people/agnes-ozman/keyIdeas/0: Tongues as evidence of Spirit baptism
people/pandita-ramabai/summary: Marathi Brahmin Sanskrit scholar who became a Christian (baptised 1883), campaigned for women's education and founded the Mukti Mission at Kedgaon for widows and orphans, where a revival broke out in 1905; she translated the Bible into Marathi.
people/pandita-ramabai/keyIdeas/0: Women's education and rights in India
people/gil-seon-ju/summary: Korean Presbyterian elder and later one of the first seven ordained Korean pastors (1907), whose public confession helped spark the Pyongyang Great Revival; credited with the Korean practice of daybreak prayer and a signatory of the 1919 March First independence declaration.
people/lucia-dos-santos/summary: Eldest of the three shepherd children of Fátima (with her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, d. 1919 and 1920) who reported Marian apparitions in 1917; she became a Carmelite nun and wrote the Memoirs that are the main source for the 'secrets'.
people/lucia-dos-santos/keyIdeas/1: Devotion to the Immaculate Heart of Mary
people/pio-of-pietrelcina/summary: Italian Capuchin who reported receiving the stigmata in 1918 and became one of the most popular and controversial figures of 20th-century Catholicism; investigated repeatedly by the Holy Office, he was canonised in 2002.
people/kathryn-kuhlman/summary: American evangelist whose 'miracle services' (from 1947) and television programme made her a leading healing evangelist; she credited healings to the Holy Spirit rather than herself and helped bridge Pentecostal and mainline/Catholic audiences.
people/kathryn-kuhlman/keyIdeas/0: Healing by the sovereign work of the Holy Spirit
people/william-branham/summary: American healing evangelist who catalysed the post-war healing revival (1946-55); his later teachings (Oneness baptism, 'serpent seed', his own role as end-time prophet) are rejected by most Pentecostals and lie outside historic Nicene orthodoxy, but 'Message' churches still follow him.
people/john-arnott/summary: Canadian pastor who, with his wife Carol, led the Toronto Airport Vineyard (later Toronto Airport Christian Fellowship / Catch the Fire), home of the 'Toronto Blessing' from 1994.
people/randy-clark/summary: American Vineyard pastor whose January 1994 meetings in Toronto started the 'Toronto Blessing'; he later founded Global Awakening, emphasising healing and impartation.
people/steve-hill/summary: American Assemblies of God evangelist, previously a missionary in Argentina, whose Father's Day 1995 sermon at Brownsville Assembly of God in Pensacola launched the Brownsville Revival.
people/joseph-ayo-babalola/summary: Yoruba evangelist whose 1930 revival at Ilesa, marked by healings and the burning of traditional objects, was central to the Aladura movement; he became the first spiritual leader of the Christ Apostolic Church.
people/simeon-nsibambi/summary: Ugandan Anglican layman whose 1929 meeting with Joe Church helped spark the East African Revival; he emphasised repentance, holiness and 'walking in the light'.
people/joe-church/summary: English Anglican (CMS Ruanda Mission) medical missionary at Gahini, Rwanda, who with Simeon Nsibambi was a leading figure of the East African Revival.
people/sadhu-sundar-singh/summary: Sikh-born Indian Christian who reported a vision of Christ in 1904, became a wandering sadhu evangelist across India, Tibet and beyond, and was famous in Europe in the 1920s; he disappeared in the Himalayas in 1929.
people/sadhu-sundar-singh/keyIdeas/3: Christ in Indian form ('water of life in an Indian cup')
people/john-sung/summary: Chinese evangelist with a US doctorate in chemistry who led revival and healing campaigns across China and Southeast Asia (1927-1940), founding many evangelistic bands and shaping independent Chinese Protestantism.
people/carlos-annacondia/summary: Argentine businessman turned evangelist whose mass campaigns from the early 1980s, with an emphasis on deliverance from demons and healing, were central to the Argentine revival.
people/gunnar-vingren/summary: Swedish-born Baptist pastor turned Pentecostal who, with Daniel Berg, founded what became the Assembleias de Deus in Brazil after arriving in Belém in 1910.
people/daniel-berg/summary: Swedish-born Pentecostal missionary who co-founded the Assembleias de Deus in Brazil with Gunnar Vingren, supporting the work partly as a foundry worker and colporteur.
people/scholastica/summary: Sister of Benedict of Nursia, consecrated to God from childhood, who according to Gregory the Great's Dialogues met her brother yearly near Monte Cassino; honoured as patroness of Benedictine nuns.
people/bridget-of-sweden/summary: Swedish noblewoman, mother of eight and visionary whose Revelations addressed popes and kings; founder of the Bridgettine Order (Order of the Most Holy Saviour), canonized 1391 and named co-patroness of Europe in 1999.
people/bridget-of-sweden/keyIdeas/1: Call for the papacy's return to Rome
people/bridget-of-sweden/keyIdeas/2: Vivid meditation on the Passion and Nativity
people/sarah-pierpont-edwards/summary: New England Congregationalist, wife of Jonathan Edwards, whose religious ecstasies in early 1742 Edwards described anonymously in Some Thoughts Concerning the Present Revival (1743) as a model of genuine religious affections.
